The Papuan frogmouth Podargus papuensis is a large, nocturnal insectivore inhabiting the lowland forests of New Guinea and northern Australia. Studies of its life history rely heavily on comparative data from its congener, the tawny frogmouth Podargus ocellatus, due to the difficulties of observing this cryptic species in the wild. For example, the age at hatching has been inferred from incubation records of the related species, indicating that eggs hatch after approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days] when incubated at a steady temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. Newly emerged chicks weigh roughly 26 grams [Ww0 = roughly 26 grams], a mass that reflects the substantial yolk investment characteristic of caprimulgiform birds. This initial weight is relatively modest compared to the ultimate size the nestlings will attain, setting the stage for a period of rapid mass gain fueled by parental provisioning. The nestlings are altricial and brooded constantly during the first week post-hatching, relying entirely on their parents for thermoregulation and food delivery during this vulnerable developmental phase.

Breeding adults exhibit pronounced sexual size dimorphism, a feature common among the Podargidae. Adult females typically reach an ultimate wet weight of 341 grams [Wwi = 341 grams], while males are larger, attaining a maximum body mass of approximately 383 grams [Wwi = approximately 383 grams]. This difference in adult body mass likely relates to the roles each sex plays in territory defense and nocturnal foraging. Females typically lay a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], containing one to two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = one to two eggs per clutch], which together constitute a notably low annual fecundity even for a large bird. This reproductive strategy is consistent with a slow life-history pace, where high survivorship of adults and extended parental care compensate for the low annual output. The pair bond is strong, with both parents sharing incubation duties and feeding the developing chick, a pattern that ensures the chick receives sufficient nutrition to grow rapidly despite the infrequent breeding events.

Developmental milestones in the Papuan frogmouth are governed by the warm, stable thermal conditions of its tropical environment. At a body temperature of approximately 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], which is typical for active, normothermic caprimulgiforms, the fledgling chick is capable of its first flight roughly 30 days after hatching [tx = roughly 30 days after hatching]. This fledging period is relatively abbreviated for a bird of its size, a trait that may help young avoid predation in the dense understory. The rapid achievement of flight capability is complemented by continued parental food supplementation for several weeks thereafter, as the fledgling refines its hunting skills. This period of post-fledging care is critical, bridging the gap between the chick's initial nutritional independence and its full mastery of aerial prey capture. The timing of fledging is closely tied to the peak abundance of large nocturnal insects in the local environment.

Reproductive maturity in this species is attained relatively late in life compared to many passerines of comparable mass. Puberty, marking the onset of gonadal development, is estimated to occur at 63 days after hatching [tp = 63 days after hatching] under the same thermal regime of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. However, the first successful breeding event is deferred considerably beyond this physiological threshold. Field observations indicate that individuals do not initiate their first brood until approximately 839 days after hatching [tR = approximately 839 days after hatching], a protracted delay that likely reflects the time required to establish a high-quality territory and accumulate sufficient body condition for the energetically demanding at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]nesting period. This deferred reproduction is a common life-history strategy in long-lived birds, where early breeding attempts may be less successful and could compromise future survivorship.

The overall longevity of the Papuan frogmouth further underscores its slow life-history trajectory. Respirometry trials have measured the maximum basal metabolic rate at 192.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 192.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] under standard conditions at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. Such a low metabolic expenditure is typical of sit-and-wait predators and contributes to the species' ability to persist on a relatively sparse diet of large insects and occasional small vertebrates. The maximum recorded lifespan for this species is approximately 5,877 days [am = approximately 5,877 days], when the individual is maintained at a typical active body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This extended lifespan, exceeding sixteen years, is exceptional among caprimulgiforms of comparable body size and positions the Papuan frogmouth as a classic example of a slow life-history strategist among Australasian birds, where high adult survival, low annual fecundity, and delayed reproduction converge.
